speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I wish to refer to a report in the press of what I said yesterday in the house concerning the Easter recess. A Canadian Press dispatch, referring to the request I made yesterday for information as to the date on which the house will rise, states:
Opposition parties indicated in the Commons today they would prefer a longer Easter recess than that suggested by the government.
The report then goes on to refer to my comments on the subject. I should like to point out that I did not ask for a longer recess. The exact words I used were:
No matter what the length of the recess may be, I suggest to the government that this is a fairly obvious consideration . . .
I was referring to the fact that members would wish to be home in the week before Easter. I wish to make it quite clear that the remarks I made did not involve any suggestion of a longer recess, but were directed to the fact that members living some distance away should know what period the recess will include. I also urged that the week before Easter should be made available to enable members to get home in time to make any necessary arrangements before Easter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make a statement on the orders of the day, but as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has raised the question at this time, I think perhaps I should make it now.
I understand that the desire was expressed to have a definite announcement as to what it is intended to propose for the Easter holiday. Since my return this morning I have received a report from our whip of his conversations with the whips of the other groups in the house. I find that among the other groups there is a decided preference for an adjournment that would start on Wednesday afternoon, the 5th of April, at six o'clock, and extend to the Monday after Easter week. In other words, the adjournment would be
from Wednesday, the 5th of April, at six o'clock, until Monday, the 17th of April, at three o'clock. This takes away one full day, but I understand that it would be much more convenient for quite a large number who wish to get home for Good Friday. I think it is; fair to assume that it will lie the desire of the house to have that done, and to proceed in the meantime in such a way so that we shall feel we have done those things which have to be done before rising for Easter. There are, for instance, four bills for which resolutions now appear on the order paper having to do with acts which expire on the 31st of March. One to which great importance is attached is that having to do with rent control. This is a very simple matter; it will provide for the extension of the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, but it will apply only to rent control. Then there is a bill to extend the time during which prices support may be provided for agricultural products, and another for the same purpose for fisheries products. There is also a bill to extend the period during which the Agricultural Products Act shall remain in force. These are matters as to which there would be serious embarrassment, chaotic embarrassment, if a final decision were not made about them before March 31.
There are three motions to set up committees which I understand most hon. members would like to see set up and organized so that, if not much can be done before Easter with respect to their work, they will be able to function as soon as we come back after Easter. They are the committees on old age security, radio broadcasting, and railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government. I would hope that we could have these matters disposed of so that the respective committees may be organized and be in a position when we return to carry out expeditiously their terms of reference.
I do not think I need make my declaration conditional, however. At this time, trusting to the good will of hon. members, I will undertake to place on the order paper a notice of motion that when the house adjourns on the afternoon of April 5 it shall stand adjourned until three o'clock on Monday, April 17.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS FROM FIVE-YEAR POOLS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS FROM FIVE-YEAR POOLS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce what payments will be made by the government to the farmers on barley and oats, and when?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO FINAL PAYMENTS FROM FIVE-YEAR POOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that at this time a statement on the whole position of payments from the grain pools should be made, and I shall make that statement now.
Last week I stated in reply to a question on the orders of the day that it had been decided not to make a further interim payment on the five-year wheat pool, but that a final payment would be made as promptly as possible after the end of the crop year. An additional payment now would have to be distributed over some 1,400 million bushels

of wheat, involving some 1,350,000 separate cheques. The cost of making such a payment is estimated at roughly $500,000. Opposition members have charged the government with having made too large interim payments in previous years, and everything considered, it seems desirable to make one further payment when the final out-turn of the five-year pool is known.
It has also been decided to make only one further payment, that is, a final payment on the oats and barley pools. This payment will be made after the end of the crop year, as soon as sales have been completed of all the oats and barley delivered to the pools.
At this time, however, I believe that I should give some indication of what might be expected by way of a final payment from these pools. Any such forecast is dependent, of course, upon a number of factors, principally the course of market prices until the balance of the 1949 crop deliveries can be sold. There are still oats and barley on farms remaining to be delivered to this year's pools, and the sooner producers can get the grain they intend to sell delivered to country elevators, the greater the possibility of the board's taking advantage of the existing market in making sales and the sooner the transactions may be closed out at the end of the crop year in order to permit a final payment. Depending upon all these circumstances, and without in any sense making a commitment that payments will be made at these levels, I think it desirable that producers should know that, based on present prospects, I now estimate final payments at 10 cents per bushel on oats, 40 cents per bushel on the feed grades of barley and 50 cents per bushel on the malting grades.
These payments may appear low compared with present market levels, but it must be recognized that sales prices were much lower earlier in the season and any merchandising organization like the Canadian wheat board must sell steadily throughout the year. Any other sales policy would not be acceptable. If current prices hold and it is possible for the board to sell the balance of the pool stocks at current levels, then the final prices realized will be higher than present estimates.
Had it been decided to make interim payments now, the amounts would have had to be set at lower levels as a matter of ordinary precaution. Rather than make smaller payments at the present time, the available surpluses will be used by the board as working capital in reducing the amounts borrowed from the banks. As I mentioned earlier, opposition members have expressed a preference for using the surpluses accumulating in the pools in this way.

In stating the prospective final payments from these pools, I have done so with the purpose of giving all producers participating in these pools an idea of where they stand with respect to their further income. I also have in mind that this information should help those producers who require credit in connection with seeding to make any necessary arrangements with their banks.
Once again I should like to emphasize the need for early deliveries from farms, and I would urge producers who have wheat, oats or barley still to be delivered to get this grain into the elevators at the earliest opportunity. There is a good demand for early shipment of all these grains; some sales will be lost if the grain is held back and some have been lost through lack of grain in position. Moreover, as I have already mentioned, early delivery of these grains will facilitate the closing out of the pools and expedite the final payments in that connection.

speechtext:
My recollection is, Mr. Speaker, that the

matter came up before the board of transport commissioners, and the board decided that it was clear that what both counsel for the applicants and counsel for the respondents requested was an interpretation of a legal problem under subsections 2 and 3 of section 32 of the terms of union. In other words, what the board was asked to do in the judgment was to give a legal opinion on the meaning of those sections.
Perhaps I could put it better this way: The point the board decided was whether or not any different rule was to be applied in the province of Newfoundland from that which was applied to the other provinces of Canada. The reply made by the board was no. The board did not decide the question whether or not Canadian National Railways was justified in making an additional charge because of the narrow gauge railway, nor was it decided whether or not the rate in question from Saint John, New Brunswick, to Halifax, as compared with the rate from Saint John, New Brunswick, to St. John's, Newfoundland, was justified. speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of this question. I have before me a lengthy report concerning this building, but I think I should summarize it and not clutter up Hansard with the three pages of details I have here.
Two years ago we had an estimate on the construction of this building. We gave notice of expropriation on the twenty-three propinquiries of the Ministry erties forming the site of the proposed building. Out of the twenty-three, two have been settled, and two will be settled in the near future. On the remainder we are negotiating for settlement. Our difficulty is that our valuators' valuations-we had two outside firms make valuations-do not agree with the amounts asked by the owners. I can give one instance without mentioning the name, so that no harm will be done to the negotiations. In one case, according to the detail I have here, we have a valuation of $10,000 for a property, but the owners are asking $60,000. It is quite difficult to come to an agreement in such a case. I am afraid we shall have to proceed through the courts.
As to the plans of the building, the sketches have been completed. They are being submitted to the two departments that will occupy the greater part of the building, that is, post office and customs; but from the list I have here I note that nearly every department of government will occupy space in the building. The moment we get the site-and we have given notice to the owners that we shall need the site from April 1 this year- we will proceed to the completion of plans and specifications, and will ask for tenders.

speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, we planned to raise the question of increased freight rates-

Before the hon. member begins his remarks, might I draw to the attention of the house the fact that almost every day, when we start on the order of business under orders of the day, there is a

Freight Rates
great deal of confusion in the house. It is exceedingly difficult under such conditions for the Speaker to hear what is taking place, and it is therefore more difficult for him to maintain order. If hon. members have business which requires them to leave the chamber, may I request that they do so as quietly as possible; or if they feel they must converse with other members, may I ask that they do that also as quietly as possible, and preferably outside the chamber.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Some time ago we thought it advisable to raise the question of freight rates. Since that time appeals have been lodged by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and by two of the provinces, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. At noon today, listening to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's midday news, I learned that seven of the ten provinces were joining together in making an appeal, I believe to the governor in council. Consequently that fact to some extent limits the discussion one can initiate or carry on this afternoon. I am going to try to keep within the bounds of the rules of procedure and to discuss this matter apart from the actual increases that have been granted by the board of transport commissioners lately. I remember-

I should like to raise a point of order, if I may, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to interrupt the thought of my hon. friend, and I am almost prompted to apologize to him for interfering with his remarks; but I think I should bring to the attention of the Speaker a matter which has been brought to my own attention only quite recently. I think the house will want to have this information before the discussion proceeds any further.
That is all right.

I would like the house to understand that I am not objecting to any discussion on the subject of freight rates, nor do I want to prevent the discussion in any way; on the contrary, I am prepared to deal with it. But my understanding is that the application to which my hon. friend heard a reference over the radio is not in fact an appeal from the judgment but is nothing more or less than an application to review, amend and vary, under section 51 of the Railway Act, the decision on the 20 per cent application. In order that there might be no difficulty about this matter I thought I should, in fairness to the house, obtain from the chairman of the board of transport commissioners a statement as to what the position is. I should like to put the statement on the record and let you, Mr. Speaker, decide; and I think the hon. member will see for himself 
what the present status is. After this letter is put on Hansard, if Mr. Speaker decides that we should go on with the discussion, I am quite satisfied; but before the discussion proceeds, I think we should have this statement before us. I asked the chairman yesterday to send me a statement, and I received it this morning.

May I ask the hon. member to make it clear to me and to the house to what body the application is being made? I understood the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to an application to the governor in council. Is the application to that body or to some other body?
Mr Chevrier: The application to which my hon. friend refers is the application which was made to the board of transport commissioners, and the decision which was handed down granting an increase of 16 per cent, plus also an application recently made by the Railway Association of Canada to increase the rates by 3-4 per cent.
Will the minister permit a question?
Yes.

I heard a very short report at one o'clock. It stated that seven of the ten provinces excluding Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland had now joined to make a protest to the governor in council. My impression was that it was an appeal to the governor in council. Already two provinces, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, have appealed to the board of transport commissioners. As I understand it, this is something new.

I am not in a position to answer that. I am not aware that there has been an appeal, save that I have seen in the press that there is to be one. If there is one, unquestionably this becomes a matter of which Mr, Speaker should take cognizance, as to whether or not it is debatable at this time.

The point I should like to have cleared up definitely is whether the present application is to the governor in council or to the board of transport commissioners. If it is before the governor general in council I would say offhand that probably there would be freedom of discussion in the house. If the application is before the board of transport commissioners, the matter would then be sub judice, since the board is a court of record and debate thereon would not be permitted in the house.

It is clear that at the present time there is an application pending before the board of transport commissioners for an

increase of 3-4 per cent, which takes the form of an application to vary, rescind and amend the judgment of 16 per cent. I should like to place this document on the record; it will give a clearer explanation from the chairman of the board himself as to where the matter stands.

I do not want to interrupt the minister, Mr. Speaker, but I am not going to deal with the 3-4 per cent increase. What I am going to deal with, if he will let me proceed, is something concerning the railway situation generally, and not specifically the question which the minister has raised. Let me point out that on March 5, 1947, a somewhat similar matter, which had arisen previously, was dealt with. On that date you yourself, sir, as Deputy Speaker, read a memorandum to the house which had been prepared by the then Speaker. It was a fairly long memorandum, and it dealt with the right of the house to discuss a matter that was then before the board of transport commissioners. The last paragraph of the memorandum reads as follows, as recorded at page 1051 of Hansard:
In making this statement, I have not overlooked the fact that the only discussion excluded by the rule is the matter actually before the board of railway commissioners, namely, an application by the railways for an increase in freight rates. I ask, therefore, that the members keep in mind the rule to which I have referred in speaking in this debate and in any debates which may follow while the matter is sub judiee.
In view of what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has read, perhaps the house would like to know just what application is before the board of transport commissioners.

Then, Mr. Speaker, if I may I shall proceed to explain to the house what is the present position. I hold in my hand a letter from the acting chairman of the board of transport commissioners, Mr. Wardrope. It reads as follows:
March 20, 1950
Dear Mr. Chevrier:
In response to your verbal request as to the present situation with regard to the application of the Railway Association of Canada for a 20 per cent increase in freight rates, I beg to state as follows:
The board by its judgment of March 1 last and for the reasons given authorized a general increase, subject to exceptions, as set out in its order No. 74034, dated March 1, 1950, of 16 per cent.
Subsequently, by application dated 10th March, 1950, the Railway Association of Canada, on behalf of its member companies as mentioned in schedule A attached to its application, has applied to the board for an order under section 51 of the Railway Act changing, altering or varying the above order in the manner set forth in the application and upon the following, among other grounds:
1.	That in its said judgment dated February 28, 1950, the board erred in not authorizing such a percentage of increase in the said tolls and rates
Freight Rates
as was required to make good the total revenue deficiency of $29,971,700 determined by the board in its said judgment and based upon the adjusted results of railway operations of Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the year 1949 which the board used as a measure of the needs of all railway companies parties to the said application.
2.	The board was in error in authorizing an increase of only 16 per cent in said tolls and rates in that such increase would have provided an increase in revenues to Canadian Pacific Railway Company based upon the traffic volume in the year 1949 of only approximately $22,300,000 instead of providing a rate of increase that would have met the total revenue deficiency determined as aforesaid by the board amounting to $29,971,700.
3.	That the formula adopted by the board in its judgment dated September 20, 1949, upon review of its said judgment dated March 30, 1948, was, according to the judgment dated February 28, 1950, given full effect to in arriving at the said deficiency of $29,971,700, but the board nevertheless made the error of further adjusting said deficiency in the manner indicated by the following paragraph of the said judgment dated February 28, 1950:
"As the majority judgment of September 20, 1949, reviewed the decision in the 21 per cent case and determined that the latter should have been 15 per cent, and also incorporated such modification in the 8 per cent interim award, it is necessary to modify the above stated deficiency accordingly."
4. That the errors above set forth constituted errors in law in that the board by its said order No. 74034, having established a total revenue deficiency for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company of $29,971,700, failed to authorize such an increase in the said tolls and rates as would make good such deficiency and thereby failed to perform its duty under the Railway Act to fix and determine just and reasonable rates and to change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation required.

Let me say first, Mr. Speaker, that I think all hon. members will agree that transportation in Canada is of fundamental importance to all the people of this country, wherever they may live. It does not matter whether they live in the central provinces, the mari-times, the prairie provinces or British Columbia. We are all vitally interested in this problem. It does not matter whether we consider it as a problem of transportation of Canadian goods from one part of Canada to another, or whether we think of it as a matter of vital interest in the defence of this country; the transportation system is a matter of great concern. Indeed, the fathers of confederation recognized this in 1867 when one of the considerations upon which confederation was achieved was the building of a railway line across the country to link British Columbia with the rest of Canada. When that was done the people of this country gave much encouragement to the transportation company which obtained the charter. They would do well to read the debates of those ten years and refresh themselves on the matters which came to the attention of parliament in those days. If they do so they will agree that there is every reason in the world why the people of Canada should view with alarm the trend which has occurred in recent years in connection with our railways and their services.
Indeed at that time, in 1880 as in 1874, it was actually the opinion of the house that the best way to deal with railway construction in Canada was to construct railways under a publicly-owned plan. But, as those who are familiar with our Canadian history will remember, that idea was abandoned, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was granted a charter. We see what amounted to a gift, if we put it in cold cash, of some $62 million, in two forms. First of all the company was granted $25 million in cash. The other $37 million was made up by the transfer of 700 miles of railway already completed by the Mackenzie government and valued at something over $37 million. In addition to that, as hon. members know, there was a grant of 25 million acres of our western lands. Again I am sure that most hon. members know that while the making of large grants had been the practice in the United States, there was one variation in that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had this advantage: that if land adjacent to the railway in one township was not satisfactory, they could substitute for it land elsewhere. In the 700 miles of railway owned by the people of Canada, I should have added, was the very valuable Pembina branch of the St. Paul and Pacific railway, which at that time was regarded as one of the most important routes in this country and indeed it is still.
I wish to get this on the record: that in addition to these grants in cash and in acres of land, they also received exemption from taxation on their railway property and on their capital stock, and exemption from customs duties on supplies they required to import.

The citation points out that the chairman ruled that the report not having been brought down, the matter was still sub judice, and the discussion could not take place. The point raised by the hon. member for Yorkton is, as I understand it, that at the present time a debate should not be permitted on any matter affecting transportation because a royal commission has been set up to inquire into that matter. I take it that that is the point of order raised.

The hon. member has quoted as his authority citation 490 in Beauchesne's third edition, which refers to a royal commission set up to deal with certain charges against a county court judge. I should like to quote from the citation:
A member endeavoured to discuss the findings of a royal commission . . . The chairman ruled that the report not having been brought down, the matter was still sub judice and the discussion could not take place.
I think the reason for that ruling was that it was a judicial matter, a charge against a judge, and that members were endeavouring to debate the findings in a report not yet brought down by the royal commission. I have never thought that because a matter has been referred to a royal commission it cannot be discussed generally in the house at the same time. I have no precedent to this effect, but there is a precedent to the effect that when a matter is referred to a committee of the house it can be discussed in the house, but the house cannot refer to the procedure and evidence in the committee before it has reported.
It seems to me that a similar principle might well govern the reference of a matter to a royal commission and that citation 490 of Beauchesne's third edition lends support to this view.
I would accordingly rule that it is not out of order to discuss transportation problems generally when such matters have been referred to a royal commission. On the other hand, I would also rule that reference should not be made to the proceedings, or evidence, or findings of a royal commission before it has made its report.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
I thank the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) for bringing the matter to my attention. It was a new question for me, and I hope my ruling meets with the general approval of the house.

When I was interrupted I believe I had just remarked that, in addition to the other concessions which were granted, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had exemption from certain customs duties on the materials required for the construction of the railway. There was the deletion of course of the provision that was in the act of 1874 to the effect that under certain circumstances the government might step in and take over the railway. Out of this gift a great railway system was established. Later, by further guarantees and by grants of land from the provinces, particularly the province of British Columbia, the financing of the railway was made possible, and indeed largely undertaken one way or another by the people of Canada.
In "The Life of Gladstone", by John Morley, there is a most interesting paragraph. In 1844 Mr. Gladstone was president of the board of trade of Great Britain, and at that time the many lines of railway were just being built in that country. Morley's "Life of Gladstone" records that:
Mr. Gladstone proposed a select committee on the subject, guided its deliberations, drew its reports, and framed the bill that was founded upon them. He dwelt upon the favour now beginning to be shown to the new roads by the owners of land through which they were to pass, so different from the stubborn resistance that had for long been offered: upon the cheapened cost of construction: upon the growing disposition to employ redundant capital in making railways, instead of running the risks that had made foreign investment so disastrous. It was not long, indeed, before this very disposition led to a mania that was even more widely disastrous than any foreign investment had been since the days of the South Sea bubble. Meanwhile, Mr. Gladstone's Railway Act of 1844, besides a number of working regulations for the day, laid down two principles of the widest range, reserving to the state the full right of intervention in the concerns of the railway companies, and giving to the state the option to purchase a line at the end of a certain term at twenty-five years' purchase of the divisible profits.
If you will read that carefully you will find much of what Mr. Gladstone tried to prevent in Great Britain occurred some forty years later in our own country.
Yesterday, I believe it was-and I think this is material to any discussion of railway problems in the house-I read a report in the press of a statement made on behalf of the Canadian National Railways by the new president, Mr. Donald Gordon. When you look back over the story of the consolidation of various lines of railway into the Canadian National Railway system you can see many reasons why it is we find ourselves faced with the difficulties that confront us today, particularly when you consider the building of redundant lines and the taking over of other facilities that were not at all remunerative. I recommend to hon. members that they procure from the library-there is at least one

copy there-the decision of a former president of the United States, who at the time was Mr. Justice Taft, in connection with the board of arbitration of the affairs of the Grand Trunk Pacific in 1921, I believe it was. Operating in this country, the Grand Trunk Pacific was found by Mr. Justice Taft to have engaged in all kinds of methods in order to deceive both the people and the government of Canada.
I am not going to go into this matter at any length, although I have before me a part of Mr. Justice Taft's reasons for dissenting from the award made in the case of the Grand Trunk arbitration. It shows how profits were concealed; it shows that when the time came for the government to take it over, values were inflated, and it indicates the manner in which this was done secretly by the board of directors in London at that particular time. Unfortunately what may be said of the Grand Trunk Railway, and its concealment of various factors of material interest to the people of Canada at the time we took over the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, is true in large part of the early history of all railways, not only in Canada but indeed in the whole of North America.
Therefore I say that from time to time these railways have been built up out of great concessions made to them by the people of Canada. For example, the Canadian Pacific, in addition to the concessions I have enumerated, have from time to time actually been relieved of obligations that they undertook in regard to some of their railway operations.
Look at the Crowsnest pass agreement, for example, under which the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia made large grants to the railway. In return western Canada was to receive certain concessions with respect to the rates on various types of commodities. If I may give a few examples, the rates on green and fresh fruits were reduced by 33i per cent; on coal oil by 20 per cent; on cordage and binder twine by 10 per cent; on agricultural implements of all kinds, set up or in parts, 10 per cent; iron, including bar, band, Canada plates, galvanized, sheet, pipe, pipe fitting, nails, spikes and horse shoes by 10 per cent; roofing, felt, boxes and packing by 10 per cent; all paint and oils by 10 per cent; livestock by 10 per cent; woodenware by 10 per cent and household furniture by 10 per cent.
Those of us who know the history of Canadian railways recall that in 1919, under the stress of war and post-war conditions, that agreement was temporarily set aside and the reductions in those classifications, together with the rates on grain then established, no longer applied. In 1922 this parliament-I

Freight Rates
remember it very well; though I was not here I followed it very closely-restored the rates on grain but did not restore the rates on these other commodities. In 1925 they were actually abolished by an act of this parliament, thereby imposing a greater burden on western Canada in the interests of the railway than it had theretofore borne. For a number of years there has been continuous propaganda on the part of the railways to get rid entirely of all that remains of that rate which was adopted as part of a definite agreement in return for grants and concessions made in 1896 or 1897.
So bit by bit we have seen our railways become more and more burdensome on the people, at least in two parts of Canada. Those two parts are the prairie and British Columbia region and the maritime regions, though to some extent the maritimes have been relieved by certain subsidies and subventions. Not only did the government of Canada make substantial money grants to the Canadian Pacific Railway, as I have said; British Columbia did the same thing. At that time these concessions were regarded as of vital importance to the very small number of people then living in the prairie region, and the not much larger number of people living in British Columbia. These rates went into effect in 1898, though the agreement was made a year or two earlier. Since that time the population of the prairie region has increased by leaps and bounds, and one would think that because of the increased volume of business the reverse would have happened and instead of the burden becoming heavier it might have become lighter.
Then, of course, these burdens have not all been spread evenly over the country. Where you have a high basic rate and an increase is given on that rate it imposes a further burden, and makes the rate still more discriminatory than it was before. That is one reason I hope that when these matters afe thoroughly considered by this house special attention will be given the matter of discrimination in our rate structure. The across-the-board, horizontal increases that have been made over the years-I am not discussing necessarily the recent increases-have imposed a burden upon some parts of the country greater than that imposed upon others. We must remember that there have been times when the cost of moving commodities from one part of Canada to another has almost equalled the value of the commodities themselves. If we look at the record of the thirties we can see how that worked out. I do not need to quote any freight rate to bring this home to hon. gentlemen. I do not need to discuss the possibility of rates being increased through
the abolition of the concessions made under the Crowsnest pass agreement. If we look at 1925, when our own parliament passed a statute settling the controversy that then existed in the country and which so many of us remember so well, the average farm price of wheat in Saskatchewan was $1.23 a bushel. In 1927 it dropped to $1; in 1928 to 80 cents; in 1929 it went up to $1.05. In 1930 it actually fell to 49 cents and in 1931 to 38 cents; someone else was in power then. In 1932 it dropped to 35 cents; in 1933 it went up to 49 cents and in 1934 to 61 cents. By 1939 it was back to 54 cents and in 1941, the second year of the war, it had only risen to 61 cents. By 1942 it was still only 77 cents. In 1947, which incidentally is the last year for which I have been able to get the average farm price from the bureau of statistics, as a result of the wheat agreements and world conditions it was up to $1.54 a bushel.
So we can see how railway transportation and the rates charged for moving commodities from one part of this country to another have a great effect on our economy. If there should be any further imposition, and particularly if we should go into a period of decline in farm prices, it might be conceivable that the cost of moving farm commodities and particularly wheat, the great commodity in which many of us are interested, from where it is grown to the seaboard might equal or even exceed the value of that commodity on the farm. That indicates how disastrous the situation would be not only for the farmers on the land but for the whole economy of the country; because I say-and I am quite sure many hon. members will agree with me-that the prosperity of this country depends in no small measure upon our agricultural production and particularly . the wheat economy of Canada. I remember hearing a statement made some years ago- speaking from memory I believe it was made by a former prime minister of this country, a former leader of the Progressive Conservative party, Viscount Bennett, but at least someone said-that no comparable group of people in the history of the world had produced as much new wealth in as short a space of time as the men and women engaged in the production of grain in the prairie provinces. Whoever made it, I believe that is a correct statement of fact. The millions and indeed billions of bushels of wheat that have been produced over the years have brought to this country new wealth exceeding that produced by any other industry or group of people in Canada. Consequently, those of us who come from western Canada are tremendously interested in this railway problem; whether it be the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific; whether it be service

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two references I should like to make to this item which deals with the welfare of Indians. According to the speech from the throne some amendments are to be made to

the Indian Act at this session. No doubt a further committee will be set up with a view to discussing amendments to the act.
I should like at this time to bring to the attention of the new minister one or two matters which have been called to my notice by various Indian bands. Before doing so however-and it is not a perfunctory duty I perform-I wish to congratulate the new minister upon his appointment to this department, particularly so as he comes from the constituency in which I was born, and also because of the fact that I know he has in this department an opportunity for service whereby he can contribute much to the improvement of conditions among Indians on the reserves.
Various representations have been made to me by Indians, who represent a very considerable portion of our population. Particularly is this true in Saskatchewan. Within the confines of my own constituency there are several Indian reserves. I have been consulted by Indian organizations representative of Indians in two or three provinces who have told me that they have certain matters they wish to have brought to the minister's attention, to the end that in any amendment of the Indian Act their rights under the several treaties made between Queen Victoria and their ancestors, and made as well in other parts of Canada between the Indians and sovereigns earlier than Queen Victoria, shall be preserved.
Generally their request is that before any amendments are brought in an opportunity be given to representatives from each province, and in particular to the representatives chosen by the chiefs of the various tribes within each province so that, at the expense of the country, they may be brought here to Ottawa and given an opportunity to make representations as to the things they wish to have done for the Indians in their respective provinces.
That seems only fair. For two years a committee-and a very good one-sat to consider Indian affairs. The Indians feel, as indicated by their chiefs and councils, that they have not had an opportunity properly to advance their claims and rights. On their behalf I ask the minister with his departmental officials to convene a meeting of one or two representatives from each province, to be chosen by the Indians in those provinces, so that they may be. brought here to Ottawa and permitted to make their representations. They believe that they occupy a position of secondary citizenship, and that they should be entitled to equality of citizenship with all citizens. About that there

In asking for equal citizenship they also ask that there shall be no interference with, or abrogation or reduction of, their treaty rights under the several treaties made between successive sovereigns and their ancestors. The fear I hear expressed among various Indian tribes is that if they are granted citizenship the advantages such citizenship would give by way of franchise, and in other direct ways, might be offset by their losing their treaty rights, their freedom from responsibility for taxation and freedom from responsibility in connection with the administration of the game laws, and the like, in various provinces.
The minister will know that there have been a number of cases before the court interpreting the right of Indians to hunt, a right guaranteed to them under their treaty rights. I was counsel in one case, which came before the court of appeal in Saskatchewan, wherein the Indians asked the right to hunt on all unoccupied land, in pursuance of treaty rights granted to them in 1873 when that portion of western Canada between Hudson bay and the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains was ceded to the crown. The court of appeal held that the treaty rights should be upheld, but that in so far as hunting and fishing were concerned those rights could be maintained only on unoccupied land.
The Indians want-and I believe they have a right to ask it-to have their rights inviolable, so that the treaty responsibilities entered into between several Britannic majesties and the ancestors of these Indians shall not in any way be abrogated or reduced by parliament. It is because they want the assurance that those treaty rights will be upheld and maintained in any amendments to the Indian Act that they ask to be given the opportunity to send representatives to Ottawa now, before the legislation is placed before parliament, to the end that their representations may be made, as they see it, to the foot of the throne, namely to the personal knowledge of the minister and his department.
I make this appeal to the minister today. I find among the Indian tribes a feeling of fear that their rights are going to be interfered with, and that those great rights which they cherish with such pride, and which were granted to them particularly by Queen Victoria, shall not be diminished by the action of a parliament in which-and I say this advisedly-because of the fact they have no vote, they have no representation. They ask that no amendments be made without first securing their consideration and approval of them. It is all very well to say that Indian

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration agents and representatives of the Indian department will be able to present to the minister and parliament the wishes and aspirations of these people, but that is not what they want. They want the opportunity to send representatives here. Ten representatives would cover all' the provinces of the dominion. They want to be allowed to come here for a few days to discuss the matter with the minister to the end that any amendments introduced will meet with their acceptance instead of being the result of the interpretation of their views to the minister by departmental officials, however efficient they may be.
Second, they believe-and I think rightly so-that the time has come when they should be allowed to take proceedings against His Majesty the King in the right of the Indian affairs department without the necessity of the issuing of a fiat which is granted by another department of the government, namely, that of the attorney general. Today the situation is that among various Indian tribes-and I am speaking particularly now of western Canada-claims are repeatedly made that there has not been that care in the administration of wards of the Canadian people that there should be on the part of certain officials of the Indian department, and that moneys in the trust funds, which should be used for the purposes of the Indians, are not used in accordance with treaty arrangements. Nevertheless, if a band of Indians find themselves in that position, where do they get when they complain? Their complaint is investigated, but they cannot take proceedings unless they have the fiat of the attorney general, and that has been refused on more than one occasion.
In my own province of Saskatchewan during the years of 1930 to 1933 one or two Indian tribes took proceedings against the crown for misfeasance and malfeasance, and one of them succeeded. From then on other tribes have been denied the right of action. They ask that they be granted the right to take proceedings for the protection of their treaty rights, and for the administration of the funds of the several reserves when and if there is anything in the nature of negligence, wrongdoing or misfeasance on the part of any of the officials of the Indian department. I do not think these are unreasonable requests. Indians are not subject to conscription or to military service in any way, but when we were at war members of the reserves in every part of Canada enlisted in numbers unexcelled by any other group in the dominion.
They ask for simple justice, and it is that appeal I make to the minister today. I say
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I
to him: Do not endeavour to have amendments to the Indian Act brought in that represent nothing more than the findings of the committee to date. In order to secure the co-operation of the Indians, above all not only must good faith be maintained with them but they themselves must believe that good faith is in fact being maintained.
It is in that spirit that I appeal to the minister not only for the welfare of the Indians but also for a recognition of what their contribution has meant to this country. I urge that when amendments are introduced they should not be piecemeal, that in fact they should represent the wishes, ideals and desires of the Indian tribes everywhere in Canada.

Before too much time
elapses after the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre, I wish to associate myself with what he has so ably said today. We have neglected our Indian population in a way which, in my judgment, constitutes a scandal against the Canadian people, and it appears that we have no intention of remedying the abuses of our ways of dealing with them at an early date. I think the time has come for parliament and the people of Canada to repent of our evil ways and bring forth fruits meet for repentance.
In addition to what the hon. member has just said, there are one or two more things I should like to mention. I see no reason why Indians should not be granted the old age pension. I believe that this neglect on the part of the dominion government is utterly indefensible. The Indians should have been the first to receive old age pensions. I believe that we should have a claims commission established to consider the various complaints which the Indians have against the administration to which they have been subjected through the years. There are violations of sacred treaties made between the sovereign and Indian tribes of Canada over 150 years ago which are simply flagrantly and callously disregarded. To call them scraps of paper, as the Kaiser called one of his treaties, does not begin to express the attitude which is maintained by Canadian government officials as to these treaties.
Something has to be done. The Indians with whom I have come in contact throughout Alberta are rapidly becoming more and more despondent, more and more disillusioned, more and more bitter. I maintain this condition must not be permitted to continue.

I want to endorse what the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Lethbridge have said. I was one of the members of the Indian affairs committee, and it has been a great disappointment to me

that nothing has been done before now after the tremendous amount of work performed by that committee. I know the committee sat each session for three years, and we had about seventy meetings at each session. It takes considerable time to go into the matter, and I do not want to do that now. I do not think a week goes by that I do not receive complaints from the Indians. It is a great problem. We set out to write a new Magna Carta for them.
The Indian problem was something that it was believed would solve itself at one time when the Indians were dying at the rate of one thousand a year. Today, with new health facilities, better hospitals and care, their numbers are on the increase at the rate of 1,500 a year. There are 135,000 Indians in the Dominion of Canada. Something must be done because a growing population like that cannot remain wards of the government. They have to take their rightful place in the economy of the country. I will speak further on this matter when the main estimates of the department come before us at a later date.

I also should like to endorse what has been said by the three previous speakers as to our Indians, and I should like to ask the minister two questions.
First, the speech from the throne indicated that the long overdue bill designed to overhaul the entire Indian Act and bring it into line with present ideas, humanitarian and otherwise, was to be introduced this session. It is not on the order paper yet, and I should like to ask the minister when we may expect that bill to be brought forward. I am sure this will represent an extensive revision of the act, and if it is to receive proper consideration a good deal of time will have to be devoted to it and I should think it might have to be referred to a committee. So the sooner the bill is introduced the better, and I think we should have some indication as to when that may be.
Then I notice that this vote is for Indian welfare, particularly supplies and material. I am glad this additional money is being provided, and that more supplies and materials are being given the Indians for welfare purposes. My second question is in connection with the welfare payments now being made to old or indigent Indians, which I believe now amounts to $8.50 per month. That is pitifully and totally inadequate, and I should like to know if any increase in that payment is anticipated or under consideration at the present time. The Indians of Alberta have asked that this amount be increased to at least $15 a month, a very modest request, and it seems to me that at this session we should

In doing so I should like to congratulate the new minister on being appointed to this very responsible office. I think the time has come when we will have to take rather forward steps in dealing with our Indian population. In my own province of British Columbia, where we have a tendency to be a little in advance of other parts of Canada-and we always tell the rest of Canada about it-we have enfranchised the Indian population. They are now on, the same basis, with respect to the franchise, as the other residents of that province. I do not think it can be very long maintained that the Indian is a citizen when he is considered as a British Columbian but a ward of the state when he comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government. While I do not believe this is the proper time to debate this issue, because the matter will come before us on the main estimates for the coming fiscal year and I also understand a bill is to be introduced, still I should like the minister to give careful thought to the matter I have just mentioned, as to whether our Indian population can be both citizens and wards of the state.

I notice the minister has not dealt with the one request I made, that coming from the Saskatchewan association of Indians, which I believe is under the chairmanship or presidency of Chief Tootoosis, an able and intelligent chieftain. He and other chiefs with whom I have consulted, not directly but by means of correspondence, have requested that representative chiefs from each province be given the opportunity to discuss the matter with the minister, and I should like to ascertain the minister's reaction to that suggestion. These Indian chiefs are very proud of their prerogatives and of their position, and are very jealous of the welfare of the people whom they represent. They feel they should be given the opportunity- not the privilege but the opportunity-of being personally represented here in Ottawa for a period of a few days in order to place their desires before the minister. They feel that too often when this is done through the regular channels the information which they wish to impart to the minister does not find its way to him; so I ask the minister if he will give serious consideration to that suggestion. Surely, in a day when we have representatives of various departments travelling over the world, whose expenses are not regarded as anything but proper expenses necessary for Canada to take her place in the world order, there can be no objection to the small expense connected with bringing these chieftains, many of whom have noble names and noble ancestors, to Ottawa to place their views before the minister, so that he in turn may be able to recommend the necessary amendments to the act. I ask him to consider this submission.

The Indians have made representations along the lines suggested. It has also been suggested by many

The Canadian government's assessment for membership in the following international or commonwealth organizations-
572. World health organization-further amount required, $48,695.

There are a couple of matters in connection with this item that I should like to raise. I believe the minister should make a short explanation about the amount required for the world health organization. I am particularly interested to know if it arises in consequence of the withdrawal from membership in the world health organization by Russia, the Ukraine and Byelorussia a year ago, thereby increasing the quotas of the remaining members of that organization.
The second matter, Mr. Chairman, is not directly related to world health organization, but I think it will expedite consideration of the item in committee if I mention it now. It has to do with the abduction of thousands of Greek children by the communist guerrillas. When the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) and I were in Greece about 15 or 16 months ago, the number of Greek children abducted by those communists, and carried across the northern borders into the communist countries to the north, was estimated in varying numbers. One figure I heard mentioned at that time was 13,000. Today I received a paper from Greece-perhaps other members of the house have received it as well-indicating the official estimate now, according to the best figures available to the government of Greece, is 23,000. They are distributed among those communist countries behind the iron curtain as follows: Yugoslavia, 11,000; Roumania, 3,800; Hungary, 3,000; Bulgaria, 2,600; Czechoslovakia, 2,200; Albania, 2,000. Those figures purport to come from the minister of social welfare for Greece.
This matter was before the United Nations at the end of November, 1948. The assembly of the United Nations condemned this abduction of children and their detention by the communist countries north of Greece. I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) if any active steps are in contemplation by the Canadian government

with a view to forcing this issue, so far as it is possible to force it upon those countries behind the iron curtain. Up to the moment apparently those countries have simply ignored everything that has been done through the recognized organs of the United Nations, in demanding the return of these children to their parents.
Of all the despicable tactics adopted by these communist guerrillas in Greece in pursuing their evil designs, even exceeding what they did in destroying villages and burning homes, the worst of all has been the abduction of children. They have been torn from their homes and carried across the border into these northern countries so that they could be reared as communists, taught in communist schools in an atmosphere of hatred, so that when they are old enough they might come back bearing arms against their fatherland. Nothing is more despicable, it seems to me, than this exhibition of savagery and brutality on the part of the communist guerrillas, who were deriving help from the communist countries to the north, and were, of course, under the inspiration and direct assistance of the Kremlin.
I know the problem is not a new one to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I bring it up now so that no one will lose sight of the matter. It is one, Mr. Chairman, that offends the elementary sense of decency of every civilized nation. I do hope, even in the face of the disregard for the expressions and demands of the organs of the United Nations by these communist countries, that something may yet be done to restore these children to their parents.

I should like to go on record as supporting the statement made by the member for Eglinton. As he has stated, about 18 months ago we were in Greece and we saw conditions exactly as he has outlined. While there, I talked with parents who had lost one, two, three or four children. At that time, I remember I thought of the abduction of the Lindbergh child in the United States several years ago, and the great amount of anxiety which that caused all over the North American continent. But that was one child. I believe that the figure covering the Greek children has grown to nearly 30,000.
I have a copy of the statement mentioned by the member for Eglinton. I realize in some small way just what these people have had to contend with during the last 7 or 8 years. At the same time, I realize the enormous problem confronting the minister of external affairs. I do believe every bit of pressure it is possible to bring to bear should, in this particular case, be exerted.
Supply-External Affairs I believe these people should have the privilege of living in a different manner from the one in which they are forced to live today. I do want to support everything said by the hon. member, and urge upon the minister that if there is any way this terrible condition can be rectified, it would be appreciated by those people who have suffered so cruelly over the years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I agree with the two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken, that among all the evil and vicious actions of the communist guerrillas in Greece and southeast Europe the abduction of the children from Greece into the communist countries has been possibly the most evil and the most vicious. As the hon. member for Eglinton has just pointed out, the situation has been discussed by the United Nations assembly on two occasions. At the last assembly we succeeded in getting through a resolution which even the communist states could not oppose. That resolution, if I remember it correctly, would have made it easier for the international Red Cross to go into those countries where these children are kept and investigate, report and help repatriate them. We hope that, as a result of that resolution, some progress has been made. What it is, I am not in a position to state at this time, although I understand the situation in Yugoslavia has been greatly improved.
I believe that the director of the international Red Cross will be in Ottawa before long. I shall then have an opportunity of talking about this matter with him, and I shall be glad to follow it up to see if there is anything more we can do. If there is, we should be happy to do it.
On the other point, the increased estimate for the world health organization has nothing to do, as I understand it, with the withdrawal of the U.S.S.R. and satellite states from that organization. It arises out of the decision at the last assembly of the world health organization in June, 1949, to increase the working capital fund of the organization. The working capital fund was devised so that the organization would have funds at its disposal during the period of the year when member states had not paid their annual assessments; and to cover that period and for the future, the assembly of the organization agreed that the capital fund should be increased from $2,553,960 to $4 million. The Canadian proportion of that, on the basis of our three per cent contribution to the organization, would be about $48,000 Canadian; and that is the purpose of this sum in the supplementary estimates.

This is a further grant to the international refugee organization. I suppose the purpose of that grant is to assist in bringing people from the d.p. camps in Europe to Canada. I have run into a rather peculiar situation that seems to exist with regard to some d.p.'s coining to Canada. In some cases their passage is paid out of IRO funds, I understand, whereas in a number of other cases the relatives of the d.p.'s pay their passage. Several cases have come to my attention. The result has been that certain people coming from the d.p. camps and settling in western Canada, and whose passage has been paid by their relatives, have found themselves in debt to the extent of from two or three hundred dollars to $1,000 in the case of some families, when they reached Canada. That is a rather embarrassing and unfortunate position for them to find themselves in when there is apparently a fund for the payment of these passages. I should like the minister to tell me if he can-or if'he cannot do so now, to find out-how many refugees from d.p. camps in Europe have had their passage paid by IRO funds and how many have had to pay their own passage or have it paid by relatives in Canada. I should also like to know if refunds can be made from IRO funds to these d.p.'s who have already paid their passage to Canada, or have had it paid by relatives.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
All d.p.'s who have come to Canada under the auspices of the IRO have been treated alike, and their expenses to Canada have been paid by the organization. That is one of the reasons we contribute to the organization. But there have been other d.p.'s who have come to Canada but who have not come under the auspices of that organization, but as a result of other arrangements, sometimes private arrangements and sometimes by other organizations. It would be quite impossible I think for us to ask the international refugee organization to pay the expenses of d.p.'s who do not come under the arrangements made by that organization; and I therefore doubt very much whether we could get any refund for the type of d.p. referred to by my hon. friend.
The amount of money in this estimate for the IRO is to provide for the increased contribution which is due from Canada because of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar last September. Our contribution to the IRO was paid in United States funds. As a result, this takes care of the increased amount required by IRO. It does not represent any additional

contribution. An additional contribution may be made next year but that has been tabled I think in the main estimates.
It may be of interest to the committee to know that because of the work of the IRO 690,000 refugees have now been moved out of Europe or from refugee camps to other countries. It is anticipated that there will be only a small number left by the end of June of this year. Of that number of 690,000, Canada has received some 77,000; Australia, 105,000; France, 36,000; Israel, 116,000; the United Kingdom, 83,000; and the United States of America, 150,000.
Has the minister the figure as to those who have come from d.p. camps under other auspices than those of the IRO?

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed, from Monday, March 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. May-bank for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company, and the motion of Mr. MacDougall: "That this question be now put."

Mr. Speaker, last night I attempted to emphasize that in the bills before us we have legislation concerned with the marketing of one of our greatest natural resources yet to be discovered. I called attention to the fact that our natural resources of gas and oil in Alberta are a national heritage, and that in so far as this government and the government of Alberta participate in the disposal of them they are trustees of the nation to safeguard their use for the benefit of this and future generations of Canadians. It has also been pointed out that these resources provide us with a great potential of cheap power which, if properly safeguarded and used in the interests of Canada, can contribute to the building of the nation.
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) pointed out, natural gas, oil, coal and the chemical industries that are dependent upon these things can make western Canada the greatest and most prosperous part of this

Alberta Natural Gas Company continent. If we combine with these great natural resources and the industries that can be built around them our agricultural resources in western Canada one does not need much imagination to realize what a great future lies ahead of that part of the country.
I want to call attention once more to just what we are proposing to do with these resources in the bills now before us. We are proposing to hand over to a company, or any number of companies that can secure charters, the right to build pipe lines for the conveyance of these resources to anywhere they choose to take them. We are giving authority to these companies to dispose of Canadian assets in whatever market will bring the greatest profit at the present time without regard to the future of Canada or future generations of Canadians who may be dependent upon their proper use. I pointed out last night that in my opinion the policy we are following is wrong. Instead of considering which route is the most economical to build, instead of considering which market will provide the greatest returns at the present tme, we should be thinking of the disposal of these resources with an eye to the future of Canada, with an eye to using them to build a greater nation. I submit that in availing ourselves of the first opportunity to market them for the greatest profit we can secure at the present time we are jeopardizing the future of Canada and the fortunes of future Canadians. In my opinion it would be nothing short of criminal if we should fail to provide for the future of Canada in order to secure immediate returns from the export of such resources. We would be failing to provide for the time when the population of the country will have increased to many times what it is now, when these resources will be the key to building great industries which will make the country a great industrial nation. I submit, as I did last night, that should be our first consideration.
I am alarmed to hear so many of those who support the measure argue from the standpoint of economy. I am appalled to find so many having as their first objective the choice of a route that can be built at the lowest cost, and the finding of a market that will give us the greatest return for these resources at the present time. Some hon. members have spoken of the necessity of maintaining good relations with our neighbour to the south. I wonder what would happen to that relationship if by following a shortsighted policy today we export these resources to United States cities and thereby contribute to the building of great industries

there which become dependent upon them for their existence. Looking ahead a few years when developments in industry within our own country require the use of these resources, we will be forced to choose between cutting off supplies to industries in a neighbouring country which have become dependent upon them for their very existence or providing for our own people. I believe that would be undermining our good relationships with the United States much more than the routing of the pipe line through Canadian territory in order to serve Canadian interests first would jeopardize that relationship at the present time.
Then the argument was placed before us that if we did not grant charters to this and other companies we would be setting up a monopoly. Some hon. members have been inclined to jeer at the position the C.C.F. party has taken, apparently in support of a monopoly. That argument has little weight as far as I am concerned. It has been pointed out already by more than one speaker that the oil and natural gas industry is a monopoly today and is liable to remain so. It has been pointed out that whether we grant charters to one or fifty companies we shall get only one pipe line. These companies, anxious to secure charters, will use those charters to milk the public instead of building pipe lines. They will use those charters to sell stock to the public, and to drive good bargains for themselves or their shareholders with whatever company eventually decides to build the pipe line. There is no question about it; the oil business today is one of the greatest monopolies on this continent; and no matter how many charters we grant we will continue to have a monopoly with respect to the construction of a pipe line through to the coast.
It has been said that if this bill should not pass this house a monopoly would be created. Well, Mr. Speaker, the sponsors of this bill have it within their power to bring in an amendment undertaking in express terms that the pipe line will follow an allCanadian route, and if that were done there would be no further opposition in this house. Practically every hon. member who has spoken has indicated that if the sponsors will state in the bill itself that the pipe line will follow an all-Canadian route there will be no further opposition. So the sponsors have it within their power to secure passage of this legislation and thereby obtain their charter any time they are ready to comply with the opinion of the majority of the people in British Columbia as expressed through the legislature of that province, or any time they are ready to comply with what I believe is the opinion of a majority in this country, and indicate their readiness to follow an all-Canadian route. If

there is to be a monopoly, if a charter is to be granted to only one company, then it is the sponsors of these bills who will be responsible for that monopoly.
The argument also has been advanced that we should let this bill go to a committee before which the principals might appear; and it has been intimated that we might secure from them an undertaking that they will build an all-Canadian pipe line. It was urged that we could get much more information in a committee of that kind. I am not too hopeful as to what we would be likely to get out of such a committee. Judging by the attitude government supporters have taken toward this bill, and having in mind the fact that such a committee would have a majority of government supporters, I do not see much hope of getting any radical amendment of this bill in committee. I believe we would get out of such a committee just what we are getting out of this house. Under the direction and leadership of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who has indicated his support of this bill, Liberal members of that committee would give this bill the same support there that they are giving it in this house at the present time. As far as I can see we would have no reason to hope for any different treatment in the committee than the treatment we are receiving here in the house. In any case, what ground is there for believing that we would get any more from a committee on this bill than we got from the committee which considered the bills passed last year? The bill under which the pipe line is being built to Superior, Wisconsin, at the present time was considered by a committee last year. Hon. members who were on that committee have stated in the house that they were given to understand this was to be an all-Canadian pipe line, and some of them were quite surprised to discover last fall that it was to by-pass such Canadian cities as Winnipeg, Port Arthur and Fort William and go to Superior, Wisconsin. What reason would we have to believe that this bill might get any different treatment?
While I am on that subject, even though the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not in the house, I want to say this. Speaking of those who insisted that that pipe line should go to the head of the lakes the minister referred to us as "little Canadians"; and I have no doubt that in his mind he considers all those who are opposing this particular bill also as little Canadians. I can tell the minister that many thousands of those little Canadians are very critical of the action of the government in permitting that pipe line to be routed to Superior, Wisconsin, instead of the head of the lakes; and many thousands of those little Canadians
