If that is not sufficient assurance, then we say once more that if that is the point which really bothers hon. gentlemen opposite, all they have to do is give us an assurance, through the sponsors of

Alberta Natural Gas Company the bills, that their companies propose to build it via the Yellowhead, and we will withdraw all objections to those bills.
The hon. member for Cariboo whose constituency would stand to gain immensely if the route is built via the Yellowhead-because his constituency is immediately contributory to the route that the pipe line would then follow -spoke yesterday.

He told us about
Christopher Columbus.

He referred to the fact that in the past the dominion government had ignored certain requests made by the provinces, particularly Manitoba, with respect to railway charters. I would ask the hon. gentleman, who seems to feel that it was not proper conduct on the part of the dominion house to ignore those requests, if he thinks it would be proper conduct on the part of the dominion government to ignore the clear, specific and unanimous request from the legislature of British Columbia that steps be taken to ensure that a gas pipe line be built via a Canadian route; because that is the issue.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-
May I ask the hon. member a question?-
I believe there is a question of privilege before the house. Do I understand that the hon. member for Cariboo rises on a question of privilege?
I would ask the hon. gentleman if the resolution at Victoria directs anybody to oppose these companies that are now coming before us.
Certainly it does.

I think the hon. gentleman has had his answer to that question. The resolution has been read on a number of occasions in this house, and I am not going to read it again now. But by necessary implication-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would take up time.
I thought the hon. member was interested in getting information.
Tell him about Alexander Mackenzie and Jacques Cartier.

The resolution asks for the Yellowhead route. It asks that the line be built via a Canadian route. One of the companies which has its bill now before the house has said in the other place that they intend to build it via the United States route. The other company in its publicity has indicated that it intends to build it via the United States route. We have not yet received an assurance in this house or anywhere else that they will not

build it via the United States route. The implication necessarily is that they will build it by the United States route if they get their charter.
The resolution makes no reference to the bill before the house.

The only way in which we can be sure that the route is built through Canada is by exercising what I submit is our responsibility as members of the Canadian parliament, and refusing to incorporate any company which does not give us the assurance that it will build its pipe-line route through Canada first.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
My time is passing very rapidly.
Question.
I should now like to refer to a matter which was raised the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing).

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Which side was he on?
Mr. Fultonr I happened to be speaking at the time. He asked me if I had any figures as to the minimum population necessary before the retail distribution of gas could be economically undertaken. Let me answer that question by asking him another one. The implication in the hon. member's question was that he-[DOT]
Will the hon. member permit a question?

The implication in the question was that, if the route did go through Kamloops, Kamloops would not get gas. Let me ask him this. If the gas line does not go through Kamloops, will Kamloops ever get gas?
Speaking in this debate yesterday the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) said, as reported at page 902 of Hansard:
Incidentally I wonder if it is fair to mention little places like Keremeos in a debate of this kind. Nothing could be crueler than to dangle before small communities the hope of cheap gas and cheap fuel and then find out that the population is not sufficiently large to justify the expense of the construction of the distribution works involved.
I say to the hon. member for Skeena that under the limitations as to the number of lines and the size of the markets, it certainly can be taken for granted that if the pipe line does not go through these areas they never will get gas; whereas if it does go through those areas there is a chance; and, incidentally, I might point out that no one in this debate, so far as I know, has stated that Keremeos would get gas. What we

have said is that if the Yellowhead route proposed by the Westcoast company is adopted a line will be built through the Merritt, Penticton, Keremeos area, and the workmen in these areas, our businessmen and retailers will get the benefit of the construction.
Oh, 200 people.
Does the hon. member think that these 200 people are not important? That is the implication in his question.
Why does the hon. member not make a speech?

I will admit that these communities of 200 people are not as large as the cities of Seattle, Tacoma and Portland, but they are of more importance to Canada and to British Columbia than any of these United States cities.
I should like to refer to the argument put forward by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) when he spoke last week. He criticized us for saying that we have the assurance that the Westcoast company intends to build via the Yellowhead route. He asked:	Of what value is any assurance
given to a committee of this house? Mr. Speaker, that is a very strange position for the hon. member to take. We have seen other hon. members take a different position in this debate, because they keep urging us to let this bill go before a committee so that we can get the people behind it there and then they will have an opportunity to give us that assurance. Yet, on the other hand, we find hon. members saying that such assurances are of no value. They may be right; but let me point out that the company which gave that assurance has now taken the next logical step, and, as an earnest of its intentions, has applied to the Alberta board for a permit to export gas via the Yellowhead route.
What about Prince George?

I will go along with hon. members this far. This is the place where we should have the assurance-we perhaps should have it from the Westcoast company. But now that we know what the facts are, this is the place where we should get the assurance. For my part I know there are many people throughout Canada, many people in my own province, who agree that we should not let these bills pass until we receive that assurance.
In spite of the obvious heat which is aroused when one considers the purely local interests in the matter, it seems to me that it is also a matter which should be dealt with
21, 1950	971
Alberta Natural Gas Company on the other level, namely, from the standpoint of national interest. This gas pipe line means a potential $100 million expenditure in the Dominion of Canada. It could mean that if it were built in Canada. On the other hand, it could mean the expenditure of some $100 million to the benefit mainly of the United States of America. I do not think that we are being little Canadians, or that we are doing anything other than what we should do in doing our duty as members of parliament in saying that so far as we can do it we shall see that that $100 million is spent here at home.
I should like to refer to the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in that connection, which were made yesterday, because I think he put the position clearly before the house. At page 904 of Hansard the leader of the opposition said this:
There are vast possibilities. In every case of this kind let us realize that cheap fuel means cheap production, and cheap production means not only the possibility of the development of new production within our own country, but also the possibility of export to other parts of the world in highly competitive lines.
And, as the leader of the opposition pointed out, that type of increased new production would go a long way towards solving the vexed question of high freight rates that now so much bedevil our industrial and transportation system in this country. Then on page 910 he summed up as follows-I ask hon. members from all parts of the house, as well as from our own province, to give these words their full value. The leader of the opposition said:
With their enormous resources, let us not measure the demands of British Columbia in terms of the gas they can use today or tomorrow, hut measure it in terms of what could happen there with their raw materials being fabricated in great industries that would use these cheap forms of fuel for the employment of hundreds of thousands, yes, possibly millions of people in that one province alone.
As he concluded he said:
Yes, we should be prepared to export our surplus, but quite frankly our policy should be Canada first in the use of the resources which we possess.
I do not see how any hon. member could fail to be, firstly, inspired by that vision for Canada; and, secondly, I do not see how any hon. member could in fact fail to subscribe to that policy. One only has to consider the enormous potentialities for Canada if this pipe line is built through Canada, and the loss that will be ours if it is built anywhere else, in order to feel himself justified in opposing to the very limit any project of which there is even the risk that the line be built in the United States, and that we may not get the benefit of it. Consider the method of construction. I understand that in connection with these lines it is not a matter of pipe
55946-62J

Alberta Natural Gas Company being sent in there already made into pipe, but rather one of sheet steel being transported to the area where the pipe line construction is taking place. Then they must have there the plant which bends the steel into pipe. It is welded on the spot. That means that there is an immediate prospect of Canadian steel companies being able to supply that sheet steel. I would be prepared to say that-
Does my hon. friend speak as an engineer, when he refers to building pipe on the spot?
The minister knows very well that I am not an engineer.
What gave you that idea?
I am speaking only as the result of the study and investigation I have been able to give to the matter.
You had better take another look.
Then perhaps the minister would tell us how the thing is built when he speaks again in debate. I am by no means an expert.
Perhaps the hon. member's information is no worse than the other information he has been giving.
Well, perhaps the minister, who knows so many things-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the man who is speaking knows so few.

-who knows so many things, but does not always seem willing to share his knowledge with the house as I know we would like to have him share it-perhaps he will make a speech and tell me how wrong I am.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not necessary.
We all know how wrong you are. You are wet behind the ears.
How big a pipe can be rolled in Canada, smart man? The only people who roll pipe in Canada-how big can they roll them?
Perhaps the hon. member for Kamloops would give way to the other hon. members.
I have one other comment I would like to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us not miss them, then.
I can say this, that I have looked into the matter, and-
Into the end of the pipe?

-I have spoken to an official of one of the steel companies in Canada, and I am told that the steel companies of Canada would be glad to be invited to tender for the supply of steel for the construction of this line. I can say that of my own knowledge.
I would say that if the line is built in Canada, there is a chance that our steel companies may be invited to tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at this rate,

But if it is built in the United States there is very little chance that our steel companies would be asked to bid. I would go so far as to say that in these projects there should be a requirement, when a Canadian resource is being transported, that Canadian steel companies must be asked to tender on the project. After all, almost a hundred million dollars is involved; there will be many millions of dollars' worth of steel in it. I understood the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are interested in conserving American dollars although it hardly seems so from their attitude tonight. I would go this far, that there should be a requirement that if Canadian bids are at all competitive with American bids, the Canadian bids should be accepted.
Here we have a chance to support a policy of developing Canada, but it calls for a positive effort. If we do not make that effort we will continue to be in an inferior position in comparison with American industry. But if we make the positive effort to conserve our resources and to enable them to be used for Canadian industry, and to make Canadian production less expensive, then gradually our industry and our markets will reach a position of equality in competition with those of the United States. But until we do that, until we take those positive steps, we cannot expect to see our industry and our markets on a basis of equality in competition with those of the United States of America.
When one considers the prospects opened up by the possibility of having this cheap fuel available for power in the area from which I come, power for the city of Vancouver, power to run our industries, power for irrigation and agriculture, power to run the pulp mills and power generally to help us develop our resources, then I say that that prospect alone would justify us in insisting, here and now, while parliament has the opportunity, that it should take the first step by refusing to allow these bills to pass until we have the assurance that this route will serve Canada

first and, having served Canada first, that our surplus should be exported to the United States. But until that is done, until we have that assurance, until we can see the possibility of the work of building Canada, which was started by the fathers of confederation, being brought to a successful conclusion by vastly developing our resources and our markets, and building this pipe line within Canada, then I say that we should not cease our efforts, and should not cease our opposition to these bills.

Superannuation and retirement benefits-
575. Government's contribution to the superannuation fund, further amount required, $63,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are back now to the item we were considering before six o'clock, having to do with superannuated civil servants.
Just before the evening recess I had reminded the committee of the figures placed on Hansard on March 16 showing the large number of retired federal civil servants whose pensions are in the lower brackets. For the purpose of drawing my remarks together I shall repeat only one figure I mentioned earlier; the others can be found by referring to what I said this afternoon. I would point out that there are 4,584 retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $80 a month. This includes in the lowest bracket of all 253 whose pensions are less than $20 a month.
Then, I would add this further item, that out of 4,338 widows of retired civil servants who are on pension, 2,516, or more than 58 per cent, are on pensions of less than $40 a month. I use this figure again, because it is the old age pension figure. It does seem to me that the committee should hang its head in shame when it is pointed out that we pay to servants of the federal government, who have been contributing into pension funds, retirement allowances less than could be obtained on old age pensions.
When the Minister of Finance has dealt with our arguments before, he has taken the position that it would be favouritism on the part of the government to supplement the pensions of these people. The minister indicated that it would not be fair to do it for them without doing it for other people on
Supply-Finance
fixed retirement allowances. I hope that all of us in the house are concerned about the security of all our old people. My position in such matters is well known, so I need not go into that at any length, but surely we have a particular responsibility as a parliament and as a government for the people who have been our employees. Surely we should be giving a lead to other people in the country who feel some responsibility for the pensions of those who work for them.
Another argument that the minister has used has been to the effect that these pensions were being paid on the basis of a contract that these persons had entered into. In other words, they had made certain payments into pension funds, and on the basis of the terms of those funds these were the amounts that they could draw out, and it would not be proper to upset that contractual relation. I want to say it is not very hopeful for the ideals which I trust the Minister of National Health and Welfare has in mind for proper old age security if that idea is prevailing in the very important part of the government that is in the mind of the Minister of Finance. What we have to consider in the whole business of dealing fairly with old people of any group, and particularly our own employees, is that having served their day and generation, having done what was their responsibility, having paid in whatever they were required to pay, when the time for retirement comes consideration should be given to their need of a decent standard of living.
It is simply impossible to justify our paying pensions of these small amounts to any number of our employees, and the tragedy is all the worse when you realize the numbers there are. I want to point out that these people are scattered across the country. They are not concentrated in any one area, which means that they are not a political force in the sense that that phrase is sometimes used. Hon. members are aware that I have risen a good many times on this matter in the house. I want to remind the house that in the whole of Manitoba there are only 386 retired civil servants and only 186 widows of retired civil servants now on pension from the federal government.
How many in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There are 186 retired civil servants and 74 widows of civil servants on federal pension in Saskatchewan. The figures for all the provinces are to be found at page 834 of Hansard of this session, and also for the United States, the British West Indies, overseas, and so on. I want to make the point-and it is true not only for myself but also for others who have taken part in the

Supply-Finance
debates on this matter on other occasions- that the number of people in our own constituencies who are affected is relatively small. Therefore we are conscious of the fact that they do not carry great political weight; that seems to be their principal handicap, but their case is just as deserving as if their numbers were much greater. When we argue on their behalf we are arguing a cause because we believe it to be just and right. The thing that has pleased me in some of the former debates on this question has been the number of members who have risen in support of this cause. I have had pretty heavy correspondence with superannuated civil servants and their associations in various parts of the country, for example, Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Victoria, and I know from this correspondence that they have been in touch with their members in this house, and were in touch with them in particular just before the election of last June. They had assurances at that time from practically all of their members that they would support their case when it was raised on the floor of the House of Commons. I hope that members of the house, and particularly those on the government side who gave categorical assurances to these people that they would support their cause and their claim for a cost of living bonus or other supplement, will implement that promise now and call upon the minister to .reconsider his position.
I have pointed out before, and I will do so again in passing, that I know of at least three .governments that have tried to do something. The province of Saskatchewan and the province of Newfoundland have both made provision for a supplement or cost of living bonus to their retired civil servants in the lower brackets. The amounts are not large in either case, but they mean a great deal to those people. Surely if these two provinces can do something like this the central government at Ottawa ought to be able to do it. The third government which I know has been trying for years to improve'the position of its retired civil servants is the government of the United Kingdom. The act at Westminster which took into consideration the fact that retired civil servants needed some improvement in their position goes back to the period of the wartime government, but it was amended a few years ago to improve the position of these people. From time to time I have asked about every question I can think of in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am glad to know that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano is aware of the fact I have been asking these questions.

I suppose it has been one of his jobs, as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, to try to find the answers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I hope he will realize that not only has he some responsibility to the minister to whom he is parliamentary assistant, but that he also has some responsibility to the people back in Coast-Capilano.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quite right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No doubt he promised he would do everything he could for them as to this matter. I see he is shaking his head the wrong way, indicating that he did not make any such promise. There were a lot out there who did, and I would suggest that if the hon. member for Coast-Capilano did not do that, the other members out there who promised to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and to do everything they could might do well to get the hon. member for Coast-Capilano on their side.
One of the questions I asked on one occasion was as to whether or not this matter had been referred to any body for advice. I was given the information that it had been referred to an advisory committee that deals with these matters. I was hopeful that would result in something, but I was never able lo get any information as to whether that committee gave advice or what it was. I was told, for example, that this simply had to be a matter of government policy. I urge the minister to reconsider the whole position.
When I rose to speak on the question at ten minutes to six this afternoon, it was not my intention to speak for more than a few minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have spoken for twenty minutes now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I felt at that time perhaps this was not the day to do this job and get the consideration it deserves. This is one of those days that we run into time and time again when time is of the essence and we are pressed to shorten our remarks, but we cannot always be expected to do that with these important measures. I felt then it might be that some of us could find a day a little later on in the session when it might be possible to go into the matter more fully. The way in which the minister dealt with the matter just before six o'clock, however, when he told me I would have two or three or four more occasions during this session to deal with it, indicating that he did not feel it needed to be taken very seriously, made me feel then that I should say a few more words, and that perhaps I might prompt others to join me in this presentation in the hope that we can yet

persuade the minister that it is too serious a matter for parliament to be paying 253 of our retired civil servants pensions of less than $20 a month, and the other figures I have given.
I insist that it is time for some adjustment to be made on behalf of these people.

May I point out to the minister that it seems to me we have an injustice here, or at least an inequity. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I gained the impression from the minister's remarks this afternoon that he was brushing aside this whole question. I realize the minister is rather apt to speak "off the cuff" like that, and does not always mean to be as tough as he sounds. Here, I think, is a case that should be reconsidered by the government.
I intend to take only a minute or two, but let me put two or three reasons before the committee. One is the difference in the value of our dollar today as compared with the value at the time most of these people made their contributions. At that time they believed their superannuation would be sufficient to enable them to live decently. Now, with the change in the value of the dollar, they find themselves getting perhaps forty or fifty per cent, in purchasing power, of what they had expected to obtain; and they have no way of improving their position unless they can persuade the government to take some steps to help them out. It is put very well, I think, in a letter I had from one of them in my own city of Vancouver, who said:
. . . our payments to the fund during our years of service are now being liquidated at 40 cents on the dollar due to the difference in purchasing power as compared to 1939. It is not by any means what we paid for.
There is this further point in their favour, that during the war years bonuses were added to civil service salaries, but apparently for purposes of superannuation those bonuses were not taken into account. As a result the civil servants who retired at that time and under those conditions have lost out as compared with others. Finally there is the fact that some of the other nations have met this situation. The United Kingdom passed legislation called the Increased Pensions Act which made some provision for retired civil servants in a position similar to that of our own civil servants who are asking that something be done at this time.
There are various other reasons, of course. There is the fact that in most cases these people cannot qualify for old age pension, and many of them are widows. But quite apart from these sentimental reasons I do think they have at least a case for reconsideration by the government, and I hope that
Supply-Finance
before the end of this session this whole question will be reconsidered by the cabinet and something done to ease the lot of these former employees of the nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the interjection I made this afternoon I had no intention, of course, of brushing off this question. I had hoped that in the consideration of these final supplementary estimates we might follow the usual practice and direct our attention not primarily to matters of policy but to the actual additional expenditures and their explanation-. I would be very happy to discuss this or any other question at length when my own estimates are called, which I think would be the more usual time to do it. We have done it in the past and I shall be happy to do it again, but I think that is really the time, not when we are asking for approval of an item of $63,000 to provide for a too-conservative estimate of the government's contribution to the superannuation fund. I realize that under the rules of the house it is open to any hon. member to raise any question relating to the superannuation of civil servants, but again I would appeal for the co-operation of hon. members in restricting observations to the actual final supplementary votes asked for here. If we attempt to cover the whole range of items I despair of being able to get these estimates through within the time I should think the committee would consider reasonable.
I want to ask a question which can be answered by a straight yes or no. Is the government paying a cost of living bonus to these civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

If we should allow these items to pass tonight without discussing them as we should, what assurance can the minister give that we will have an opportunity to discuss them later? I remember that last session I agreed to such a request for some reason or other, thinking I could bring up the matter at another time, but I never did have another opportunity. We should have some assurance right now that if these items go through tonight we shall have every chance to discuss these matters later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can only give this assurance, that for the past two or three weeks my colleagues and I have been trying to get down to -a discussion of the main estimates for the coming year. The house, within its rights, has preferred to make speeches on general questions rather than consider the details of the expenditures. My own department is now before the committee. I shall be happy at as early a date as possible to get down to a discussion of the details of the department,

Supply-Finance
which happens to deal with this matter of superannuation. There is a very large item in my estimates covering the contribution by the government to the superannuation fund. That goes for the other departments as well; but it simply cannot be done if the house is not willing to co-operate. Without desiring to offend anyone, I suggest that that really depends upon the desire of private members to get down to a consideration of the details of the estimates and not take too much time discussing general principles on individual items.
I reiterate, however, that tonight we are considering the final estimates of the year, the estimates which traditionally make provision for cleaning up liabilities already incurred under existing votes in which, for one reason or another, there was an underestimation. There will be, first, the opportunity on the main estimates; second, an opportunity on the main supplementary estimates which are usually brought in two or three weeks before the end of the session; and finally an opportunity to discuss special matters on the final supplementaries at the end of the fiscal year. So there are at least three opportunities; but I repeat that it is in the hands of the house. Nothing would please the government better than to get down to a consideration of the expenditures item by item; but what happens? We have an item here of $63,000 which is really a vote to cover a too-conservative estimate of the contribution of the government to the superannuation fund because there were more promotions, or more people retired, or for some other reasons. Instead of considering whether the Minister of Finance was right or wrong in his estimate, however, we enter upon a debate upon the desirability of superannuated civil servants receiving some addition to their superannuation. It is within the rules, of course, but it is not taking into consideration the particular item of expenditure now before us. That is all I can say.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just a word-
Sit down.
That is exactly what happens when we are on the estimates; we are told to sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That doesn't bother me.
The minister will recall that when I rose before six o'clock the words I used and my whole tone of voice implied that I was giving him fair warning that we were going to deal with this at the proper time. It was only because of what I thought was the offhand attitude the minister took toward the matter that I felt that warning needed to be driven

home, and I trust we have done that effectively.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can say is that I very seldom hold up my own estimates, but I must have done that by my interjection before six o'clock.

I am not trying to hold up the estimates, but in spite of the teacher's lecture I want to ask this very simple question. Are the mounted police concerned under this item, when the main estimates are being considered? I want to talk about them at the proper time, which I think is not now.

speechtext: I am sorry, but there was someone speaking behind me, and I did not hear my hon. friend's question.
I was wondering if the superannuated mounted policemen come under this gen eraT item when we come to it? I am not going to speak on it now, but I am then.

institution that can pass a law to stop the fish from going from North America to Norway. I think the easiest way to get a depression is to preach about one. speechtext:

maintain this establishment I would judge that the government will look after the upkeep of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will be dealt with properly, and will be maintained by the Department of Public Works and kept in a good state of repair.

I hope that when the minister is considering the upkeep of the Prime Minister's home he will also consider the home of the leader of the official opposition, because I think they should both be looked after by the government.

May I ask the minister to raise his voice a little? We could not hear his recent answers over here. Did I understand him to say the price paid by the government for this property when they acquired it about four years ago was $135,000? A question was asked about the original cost. I take it the answer did not relate to the original cost of the construction of the house, but to the original cost to the government when it acquired the property. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The government proceeded by way of expropriation in this case, and evidence was heard before the exchequer court. I cannot recall the exact amount, but speaking from memory it would be somewhere between $130,000 and $140,000.
Then trying to see the picture whole, to the $130,000 we add something like another $130,000 to date, so that the cost to date runs in the neighbourhood of $275,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. This is an estimate for $35,000 which is the amount that we expect to spend before the 31st of March of this year. We have retained as architects the firm of Allward and Gouinlock of Toronto. As to the estimate of the total cost, nobody before starting work on the building could give a final estimate of what the cost would be.
I think the minister mentioned another item of expenditure earlier as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was a year or two ago. It was expropriated four or five years ago.
We have the $130,000 to $140,000 to which the minister has referred and then this item of $35,000, but if I heard the minister correctly he said that there was another item as well of $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was asked the question whether I could give an estimate of what the work will cost on this residence. I said that I am told-and this would not be final- that it will amount to some $135,000.
Then the total cost to the government by the time the property has been completely renovated will be about $275,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not give any definite figure. Personally I do not know because I have not found anybody yet who can give a final estimate of the cost.

Mr. Chairman, no one in this house criticized the idea of acquiring a home for the Prime Minister. When the announcement was made in the house by the then acting prime minister a reservation was made by some as to the selection of this particular property for the purpose. The question will be present in the minds of many members as to whether this was the best residence available at the cost. I am bound to say that it amazes me as a member of the house that the government has embarked upon this project without having some idea of the cost of renovation before they started.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister has given it to you.
The Minister of Public Works, a very experienced minister, has just told us that he did not even at this stage-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member will admit that we are now discussing an item of $35,000 for repairs, alterations and improvements to the Prime Minister's residence. I do not think the hon. member should go back and question the decision as to whether this or another house should have been bought.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that I am entirely in order in trying to get to the bottom of this project. Here we are asked to vote another $35,000-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I appreciate that the decisions of the chairman are not always satisfactory to hon. members, especially when they want to advance a certain point of view; but in my understanding of this discussion the hon. member is out of order when he raises the question on this item of whether the government should have bought this property or another.

I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Eglinton was not discussing whether the house should have been bought. He is trying to get at the total amount it is going to cost, and I submit that is quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to give as much latitude on this item as may be permissible, and so far I believe I have done so. I am simply warning the hon. member for Eglinton, when he says the
Supply-Public Works
minister should not have gone into this project without having any idea of the cost, and makes statements of that kind, that we are now discussing an item of $35,000 for repairs, alterations and improvements. That is all I am doing at the moment.

Before you make any ruling, Mr. Chairman, I want to make it quite clear that what I am talking about now is this item of $35,000. The considerations I am putting forward are strictly relevant to the question whether this house should provide $35,000 when, even at this stage, the minister is not able to give us an estimate of the final cost. Apparently the government has just gone ahead without doing what any sensible member of this chamber would have done, that is, finding out what it was going to cost before commencing the project. It amazes me that at this stage, in March, 1950, nearly a year after the decision was made to take this property and renovate it for use as a residence for the Prime Minister, the government cannot give us an estimate of the total cost of the entire undertaking. I have tried as best I could to get the figures and put them together. When we do add up the figures the minister has given us, he will not commit himself in any degree to the total we arrive at.
I am in complete accord with the idea that a suitable home should be provided for the Prime Minister of this country; let there be no mistake about that. At the same time, as a matter of common sense and ordinary sensible business practice I believe the government should know the cost of a project before it undertakes it. Obviously that was not done in this case, and I think it is a ridiculous way of doing business.
I am going to ask this further question-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before you use that word "ridiculous"-
I ask the minister to give us-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Eglinton has the floor.
I am trying to facilitate the minister's reply by saying there is one other question I wish to ask.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You will not facilitate anything by calling this ridiculous.

I certainly will call any practice ridiculous under which a government blithely goes ahead with a project of this size without having any idea in advance of what the cost is going to be. If I understood the minister's statement correctly, that is precisely the situation that confronts the government and the rest of us at this moment.

Supply-Public Works
The other question I want to ask the minister, if he will be good enough to try to shed some light on it, is this. Are the figures which have been given to us the cost of the renovation of the property, or do the figures he has given include the cost of suitably furnishing the residence?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The best answer I can give is in a report I have here. Believe it or not, I took this as good advice from my officials:
Due to the nature of the work involved, the age of the building and the impossibility of determining the structural condition of the building until the work was under way, it was not possible to arrive at an accurate estimate of the total cost. The department therefore considered that a contract on a basis of cost plus a fixed fee would be the most practicable. Negotiations were entered into with Alex I. Garvock Limited1, who offered to perform the work on a basis of cost plus a fixed fee of $10,000-
That amount I am sure of; we know that. -such fee to include the provision of all supervision of the workmen, the engaging of a superintendent satisfactory to the department, and the provision of workmen's tools and equipment required on the work which are ordinarily supplied by the general contractor.
I know what it is costing for this contractor; we will have to pay $10,000, and he undertakes to do this work. Being no expert myself, I find that even these people cannot give me a final or definite estimate; but I am told that it will amount to something in the neighbourhood of $135,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps it will help my hon. friend if I add that an additional $80,000 is provided in the main estimates for 1950-51, which were tabled some time ago.
The minister has not dealt with my final question, as to whether any provision is made here for the furnishings.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In which figure?
In either figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
In other words the figures the minister has given simply represent the cost of the structure as renovated?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Then I come back to my other point. Were not the considerations set out in the report the minister has just read available to the government before they selected this particular property for the Prime Minister's residence? I should have thought that, faced with such a situation, that is to say, complete uncertainty as to the eventual cost of renovating this large property, the government would have asked themselves whether they could not do better with their
[Mr. Fleming.!
money by buying another property, or by building a new home on this site instead of renovating a house that I am told is many years old. Will the minister give us some further information on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The government gave a great deal of thought to this project, and came to the conclusion that this was the best way to acquire and have a home for the Prime Minister of Canada.

The reason I brought this up in the first place was that I have heard it said by architects and others interested that it would have been better, and would have provided a better building at approximately the same or at least a known cost, if the house were torn down and a new house built. I wondered if the department had considered building a modern house instead of trying to renovate the old house on this site. As everyone knows, this is an admirable site for a home for the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was discussed for I do not know how long. Every angle was gone into, but we came to the conclusion that having that site and the shell of this building we owned, it would be a proper way to proceed to provide this residence.

600. Departmental administration-further amount required, $2,500.

I notice that this item is called "resources and development". I should like to say a word or two about the development of resources. I think everyone recognizes now that in the province of Alberta we have probably the finest resources of any province in Canada. Those resources have been there for hundreds of years; they have been there ever since people went to Alberta. We have

not been able to develop them until recently. Now, there are several reasons why that is so, and one of the largest considerations entering into the development of our resources today is the cost of doing business.
In this connection I desire to register an emphatic protest against the freight rate structure in Canada, particularly as it applies to western Canada. The freight rate structure is particularly important, because of the prevalence of the non-discrimination-in-trade philosophy in government thinking, which is leading the government to think that every industry ought to stand on its own feet. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance was correctly reported, or whether I remember exactly what I read, but it seems to me he used one of those breezy, dramatic expressions of his not long ago, that our industry in Canada has got to brace itself for competition abroad. Whether he said that or whether he meant it, I do not know but I fancy he meant it. The point is that, not very long after he made that remark, his government was party to permitting a thing to happen in Canada that increased the difficulty of every industry in Canada in bracing itself against competition from abroad. Now if you put enough difficulties or enough burdens on a man's back, he cannot brace himself against anything. He falls of his own weight.
In this connection, the freight rate structure is exceedingly important in this country. It increases production costs at the very time when we should keep production costs down. Then there is an excessively high cost of living today. It is a burden that is pushing the people of Canada right to the ground. I believe from coast to coast the Canadian people are literally groaning in misery. Not very long ago there was an increase in the price of coal in Ottawa, and the people just groaned. What was partly responsible for that increase? Things like the increase in freight rates-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but may I point out-
If the chairman would speak a little louder, I could hear him.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I said I was sorry to interrupt the hon. member, and I am sorry if I did not speak loudly enough for him to hear me. The item I have before me is item 600, "resources and development, departmental administration, further amount required, $2,500." I fail to see how the hon. member can discuss freight rates under this item, but perhaps that is not what he was talking about. Perhaps I did not hear him too well up here.
Supply-Resources and Development
I thought I made it quite clear to the chairman when I began, that I was laying emphasis on the second part of the title, which is development of resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if I could appeal to my hon. friend? This item actually covers an additional amount for printing and stationery of $1,000, and an additional item of $1,500 for travelling expenses. Tomorrow is private members' day and Thursday, for reasons with which the hon. member is familiar, I am unable to be in the house. As I indicated earlier, it is urgent that these estimates should, if possible, be passed tonight. I would appeal to him, if it were possible, to defer his remarks on the general subject of resources and development until a little later in the week, or perhaps some time next week.

I believe every member in the house, and the minister himself, will agree that the development of the resources of Canada is going to depend a great deal on the sort of freight rates that prevail in Canada. I fancy, therefore, I am quite in order in that respect. I realize the difficulties under which the minister is labouring, and I deeply sympathize with him; every member in the house does. We sympathize with him, not only because of the difficulties he is in with respect to having these estimates passed, but because of certain other difficulties. At the same time, I feel the discussion of freight rates has been deferred too long. I think it is time that the members who represent the provinces that are being victimized spoke out, every one of them.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to see that one hon. member is catching the spirit. It is not my desire, Mr. Chairman, to hold up the house unduly. I believe I have nearly said enough to express my point of view, but I should like to add a few words in a general way before I sit down.
I should like to excuse myself on another score. This amount of money we are discussing falls under item 600, which is departmental administration. From time immemorial it has been customary in British houses of commons for the widest latitude to be allowed in discussing the item of departmental administration. I do not have to have much latitude to get a freight rate discussion out of the development of our natural resources.
Before the chairman felt compelled to interrupt in that genial way of his which we all admire so much, I was going to point out that Canada needs a tremendous amount of population today. We are never going to get population into this country, and have it

Supply-Trade and Commerce remain here, unless we make it possible for the people in Canada to live. What we have been doing up to the present moment, and what we have been doing ever since I can remember-that is about 40 years in Canada -is having children; raising them and educating them; and then sending them to the United States. 610. To reimburse the Canadian wheat board for expenses incurred from August 1, 1948, to July 31, 1949, in the administration of delivery quotas and permit regulations, etc., $96,455.
I had hoped that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might be in his seat now, but I see that he is not there at the present time.
He was here a minute or so ago.

The Minister of Finance is here, in any event, as is also the Minister of Agriculture. Under this Canadian wheat board item, I want to refer to the statement made earlier today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that ten cents a bushel will be paid out on oats this year and forty cents a bushel on barley. The minister went on to say that one of the reasons no payment would be considered on wheat was the attitude taken by the opposition. I hope he was not referring to my attitude. I at no time objected to the twenty cents having been paid last year. My objection was rather to the fact that when this amount was paid the farmers were not told the actual financial position of the wheat board at that time; and from statements of the Minister of Agriculture and others they assumed there would be a substantial payment this year.
My question is this. I should like the Minister of Agriculture, if he can, or the Minister of Finance-who I am sure know the financial position of the wheat board with respect to wheat just as they do with respect to oats and barley-to tell this committee and the farmers of western Canada approximately how much the payment on wheat is likely to be after the conclusion of this crop year. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out this afternoon, the farmers must undertake certain credit; and in doing that they would like to know the payment they will receive for oats and barley. I am not asking the minister to go out on a limb, but surely he can estimate reasonably closely the amount the payment will finally be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here. He had expected that we would reach his estimates earlier this evening and he had to leave. I believe he will be here tomorrow. I will

bring my hon. friend's question to his attention. I am not in a position to make an estimate; and for the reasons which the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave this afternoon, I do riot believe any other minister is. All I can do is to bring my hon. friend's question to the attention of the minister, and he will try to deal with it tomorrow.
Would the Minister of Agriculture not care to make a guess?

This is not a matter which is under my department at all. It is a matter which is under the Department of Trade and Commerce and always has been. The statement has been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Here is the Minister of Trade and Commerce coming into the chamber now.
In reply to the hon. member's question, the substance of which has been conveyed to me by my colleague, may I say that I have no idea.

I cannot accept that statement. In the past the Minister of Trade and Commerce has never been bashful about making forecasts. The wheat board is under his department, and I am sure he knows its financial position today and can make a reasonably good estimate of what the final payment will be. I am sure the farmers would like to know. For example, if a farmer over a five-year period had marketed 20,000 bushels of wheat-which is a quantity of wheat that many farmers would have marketed-and if the payment is twenty cents a bushel, the farmer will get another $4,000; if it is ten cents a bushel, he will get $2,000. All I am asking is that the minister make an estimate so that the farmers can plan their business this year in the light of the payment they can anticipate.

I should like to follow up this question for just a moment or two, and I will not be long. The other day I had on the order paper a question which had to do with the marketing of the 1949 crop up to date, and I was told that it was not in the public interest to give the trading position along certain lines on which I was asking the question. If that question had been answered as I asked it, we would have been in a position to know fairly closely what the next payment should be, at least; not what it would be, but what it should be. But I was not able to get that information. I think the attitude of the minister at this time is most unfair. I want to ask another question that deals with the item of approximately $96,000 for administration of delivery quotas and

Supply-Trade and Commerce permit regulations. Has that to do with field inspectors? If it has, I should like to know how many of those there are.

612. To reimburse the Canadian wheat board for the deficit incurred from the operations of the wheat board on the 1948 crop account, flax division, for the period August 1, 1948, to July 31, 1949, pursuant to order in council P.C. 3376 of July 28, 1948, $3,884,182.

This item has to do with an amount of almost $4 million on flax account and I think the minister should explain why that is. That also raises another point I want to mention. I had on the order paper a question which was answered at page 833. It had to do with the federal grain elevator at Saskatoon. I have now on the order paper another question asking for much more detailed information; but on the information I received, it cost the government over $78,000 to operate that elevator last year.

Supply-Trade and Commerce On the average by month, there was only a shade under 12,000 bushels of all types of grain stored there. That is a gigantic cost to somebody. The point I want to make about this flax is this, and I raised this issue with the minister throughout the war years, when the government was spending a great deal of money on crown companies and so on, and in assisting other companies. Whole processing plants were built in eastern Canada where your flax had to be taken east and processed and much of the processed article was taken west again, especially in the matter of feeds for livestock. Since then the farmers themselves have set up an organization and developed a processing plant at Saskatoon. I have been credibly informed that that plant had to close down last summer because there was not sufficient flaxseed and such like materials available in the west, because that flax and processing cereals had been moved east at that time. Naturally the cost would be too much to transport it back west.
Surely, with the grain and with an elevator such as that in Saskatoon, there was a great lack of co-operation somewhere between federal government departments, and certainly a vast waste of money. The building in Saskatoon cost over $1,500,000 to construct to begin with, and they are spending around $78,000 a year for administration, and have been for the last five years. They refuse to spend money to develop an industry that should have been developed where practically all of the flax is grown. Some of this processed material had to be shipped back west. I hope the minister can give an explanation of this huge expenditure to take care of the flax for that year. I pointed out what happened to the elevator in Saskatoon, and the lack of material being stored there last year.

The explanation of this item is that for the crop year 1948 the government guaranteed a price of $4 per bushel for flax marketed in that year. A very large crop of flax was grown, and while it looked like a safe price at the time it was set-it was a dollar below the guaranteed price of the previous year-suddenly instead of there being an active demand for flax there was no demand at all except for domestic sales, with a very little for export. The result is that the wheat board was not able to market in the year 1948 any more than a small part of their flax crop. Owing to a small crop last year the board is gradually disposing of the surplus. This amount is required to pay the carrying charges on the flax that was taken in, and to write the crop down to its current price of $3.80.
[Mr. Ross (Souris) .1
As for storing flax in Saskatoon, the purpose of the wheat board is to market grain, not to store it. Storing is only incidental to marketing. Saskatoon is not a marketing point for flax, and it was moved to the market. It was the duty of anyone who had a crushing plant in the west to make arrangements with the board to store flax in Saskatoon, or to move it anywhere else, and arrangements could easily have been made. That was done to the extent that the arrangements were made, but nevertheless the board cannot run the business of the crushers. It can only market the farmers' grain to the best advantage, which is the work delegated to the wheat board.
Is it not true that at the time the crushing plant at Saskatoon was short of flax the wheat board was paying storage for that same flax in some of the large elevators in the east?
It may be.
I think the answer is not "may be" but "yes".

I would think the same situation is true of wheat. I understand that that elevator has a storage capacity of considerably over 5 million bushels. I say to those people who are very much interested in the Hudson bay route that this would be the place to store wheat as well as flax. There will have to be much more explanation of the matter than that given by the minister. I understand that there were less than 12,000 bushels on the average stored during all of last year in a building owned by the government with a storage capacity of over 5 million bushels. I understand that the wheat board will have quite an item for storage at the head of the lakes. At the same time their own building is standing out there idle throughout the year. There should be some explanation of that situation.

Mr. Chairman, we are losing export sales on wheat today because we cannot get enough wheat in marketing position. My hon. friend knows enough about wheat to know that marketing positions are Vancouver, or the head of the lakes or an eastern shipping point. Saskatoon is not a marketing point. Any grain stored there would be out of position and would cause that much further loss of export sales.

speechtext: I understand the hon. member wishes to speak to item 614?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That refers to the Chalk River project, capital and operating expenses, $200,000.

Yes, and that is exactly the item I am talking about. So far as I am concerned, the amount required in this vote, for the purposes for which it is intended, receives my hearty approval. I am completely in accord with it. At the same time I do not think these two matters can be separated to any great extent.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was permitted to make a suggestion that a committee should be set up to supervise, scrutinize and report to the house concerning matters which may come within the scope of this vote. It is concerning the remarks of the hon. member that I wish to speak. I say that a committee of that kind at this time is not one which would meet with my approval. In my view the time has come when we should get down to considering a main committee on defence.

speechtext: Order. When the chairman rises it is one of the rules that hon. members must resume their seats. I see now that the hon. member has done so, and I thank him for it. I believe I heard him say that he is in complete accord with item 614. Shall the item carry?

speechtext: Then I would ask the hon. member to relate his remarks to the item under discussion, and not speak about national defence.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I do not wish to be bothersome, or to delay the Minister of National Defence in having this item passed. I will repeat what I said earlier, that I agree with the principle behind this item. However, if we wish to discuss it in detail, in all its ramifications, it will take a long time. I have no intention of doing that either-and I am not going to talk this out, until eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member would allow an interruption. As I indicated earlier, there is some importance in passing a supply bill, including two of these items, today, if possible. It is impossible for me to be here until Friday. Tomorrow is private members' day. If I could have unanimous consent to a motion to sit a few minutes after eleven o'clock, I would hope that we might be able to conclude by that time. However,
I appreciate the fact that to do so I would require unanimous consent. I would appreciate it personally if such consent could be given, because hon. members will understand that I have heavy commitments between now and next Tuesday when the budget is to be brought in. It would be a great accommodation if this procedure could be followed.
I can complete my remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then if I might put the motion now to sit after eleven o'clock-
All I want to do is to ask a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would need a motion, anyway.
If you want to; I will do anything to accommodate you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would make the motion to sit after eleven o'clock, if I could have unanimous consent-in the hope that it would take only a few minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Only for a limited time. So often we grant a few minutes, and we are here for an hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should hope we might do it by 11.15. We have a few more items to pass, all of the usual year-end variety, to pay bills. Then we have to put through two bills founded on the interim supply. I should hope to conclude that.

I am quite prepared to sit as long as required, and I wish to have that understood. But I also wish it definitely understood that these are not just a few items to be dealt with. There are two very important items here which have not been discussed previously. One of these amounts to $42 million and the other to $4,317,000. I certainly intend to direct a number of remarks to the latter item, because it is the first time it has been before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should hope we might sit a sufficient length of time to dispose of these, and would ask if the house would be prepared to do that. Of course, I am not in a position to insist. However, it would greatly facilitate the job I have to do if that consent were given. We have had close to five hours of discussion now.
It will be just as easy, with unanimous consent, to take it tomorrow.
I have no objection to sitting fifteen or twenty minutes, but I am not going to sit here, if there is going to be a discussion, until twelve o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then may I suggest this: tomorrow is private members' day, on resolutions, I understand. If I could have unanimous consent to complete this job at three o'clock, perhaps it would suit the house better. I would appreciate it very much if that could be done.

Agreed.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
